_readme: Every model parameter, with low/mid/high values and its source. The sim runs at all three and reports ranges. Parameters marked calibrated are fit only on the calibration corridors (ditmars, park_slope_5th) by validation/calibrate.ts; holdout ground truth is never read by /sim.

bprAlpha.source: Bureau of Public Roads (1964) volume-delay function; 0.15/4 is the standard FHWA default, 0.10-0.30 the range used in practice for urban arterials.

bprBeta.source: BPR (1964); beta 4 standard, 5 used for congested urban networks.

laneCapacityVph.source: HCM base saturation flow ~1,900 pc/h/ln times typical urban signal green ratio g/C 0.35-0.50 for arterials; lower for local streets with parking and unsignalized friction.

defaultPeakHourVolumeVph.source: Used only when no NYC Automated Traffic Volume Count is within 500 m (flagged 'estimated'). Order-of-magnitude two-way peak-hour volumes by OSM road class for dense US cities; NYC ATR counts near the corridors (sim/assets/*/context.json) fall in these bands.

arterialOriginWeight.source: Trip ends weighted toward arterials (CLAUDE.md Section 4); relative weights are an assumption.

sampleTrips.source: Monte Carlo sample of OD pairs per area; scaled to calibrated volumes.

peakHourShareOfDaily.source: FHWA Traffic Monitoring Guide: urban K-factors typically 8-10%.

closureHoursPerDay.source: NYC Open Streets typically ran ~8am-8pm on operating days; SF Hayes Street weekend closure is ~10-15 h.

baseVolumeByClassPph.source: Prior for hourly pedestrians on a block face in a dense neighborhood; NYC Bi-Annual Pedestrian Counts (cqsj-cfgu) on commercial corridors are typically hundreds to low thousands per hour. Flagged 'estimated' where no count within 500 m.

perBusinessPph.source: Added hourly pedestrians per active storefront on the block (business density drives foot traffic); assumption checked against NYC ped counts where available.

closureUplift.note: Multiplier on the fitted uplift; the mid value is set by calibration.
closureUplift.source: Fit on calibration corridors. Prior literature: NYC DOT plaza evaluations report 10-40% more pedestrians; car-free streets in Europe report larger gains.

seatingMultiplier.source: Whyte, The Social Life of Small Urban Spaces (1980): sittable space is the strongest predictor of people staying. Applies to dwell and capture.

programmingMultiplier.source: Events/activation raise attendance; Project for Public Spaces 'Power of 10'. Assumption.

captureRate.source: Share of passing pedestrians who become customers, by category. Retail capture-rate rules of thumb (2-8%); food & drink highest, appointment services lowest. Assumption.

carCustomerShare.source: Share of customers arriving by car on NYC neighborhood retail corridors: NYC DOT / Transportation Alternatives merchant-intercept surveys report roughly 5-20%.

carLossElasticity.source: Fraction of car customers lost per unit of added access difficulty (closure of frontage + added delay). Assumption.

outdoorSeatingCapacityGain.source: Added seated capacity from roadway dining relative to indoor capacity, for food & drink on closed segments. During 2020-21 indoor capacity was restricted, so roadway seats mattered more.

diversionFromNearby.source: Share of newly captured visits on the closed street that are diverted from nearby corridors (the control). Assumption; nets the 'zero-sum' critique.

dwellMinutesBase.source: Average time a passer-by spends on a block face; walking a 100 m block takes ~1.2 min.

dwellFoodMultiplier.source: Each food & drink share point raises dwell (people stop to eat). Whyte: 'If you want to seed a place with activity, put out food.'

encounterRate.source: Probability per person-minute of co-presence that two lingering strangers start a conversation, scaled by density. Assumption (Whyte 'triangulation'); interaction is model output, not validated.

thresholds.source: lingerIndex = people present per 100 m at any moment. Whyte observed well-used plazas sustain dozens of sitters; below ~8 a space reads as empty (the 'empty plaza' effect).

connectionShare.source: Share of street conversations between strangers that become a repeat acquaintance (recognised next time). Assumption informed by research on weak ties and 'familiar strangers' (Milgram 1972); model output, not validated.
